At that unit decline, price growth of 6.0% would imply a 5.02% sales decline. I forecast pricing keeps March above the threshold but fades enough for a June-quarter crossing.

Dover's 2022 bookings fell 11.1% to $8.3 billion while reported revenue rose 7.6% to $8.5 billion. Pricing contributed approximately 6.9% to revenue (A, B, D). I forecast existing orders support March revenue above the threshold, then fewer replacement orders pull June revenue down at least 5% year over year.

December product sales rose 38.6% as Star passed through a 54.4% increase in wholesale cost per gallon. Star says high heating costs prompt conservation and customer losses (A, B). I forecast price pass-through keeps March consolidated revenue growth above -5%, then wanes enough for lower gallon sales to drive a June decline of at least 5%.

Union Pacific's 2022 freight revenue rose 14% on just 2% volume growth, helped by fuel surcharges and pricing. Domestic and parcel demand softened in the fourth quarter (A, C). I forecast pricing keeps March above -5%, then weaker shipments and lower year-over-year fuel surcharges push June consolidated revenue down at least 5%.

Higher fuel recovery, export coal rates and the inclusion of Quality Carriers helped lift CSX's 2022 reported revenue 19%, even as chemical and export coal shipments fell (A–C). I forecast those revenue gains keep March above -5%, then smaller fuel and coal rate contributions expose the shipment declines and take June to -5% or below.

Saia's 2022 revenue rose 22% despite 0.8% fewer LTL shipments per workday (A, B). March still compares partly against dates before the January 24, 2022 rate increase of 7.5%. June compares entirely against the higher rate (D). I forecast March stays above -5%, then shipment weakness and a smaller fuel surcharge contribution push June to -5% or below.

Fuel surcharges supplied $417.7 million of Schneider's $995.7 million reported revenue increase, about 42%. Network volumes were already falling amid weaker demand and reduced productivity (A, B, D). I forecast dedicated volume gains help keep March above -5%, then lower surcharge revenue and continued network volume losses drive a June decline of at least 5%.

December net sales grew 12.0% because a 25.0% increase in average unit price offset a 10.4% unit decline, concentrated in direct ship (B, D). At that unit decline, price growth of about 6% puts sales at the −5% threshold. I expect pricing to keep March above the threshold and provide less protection in April–June.

Reported revenue growth slowed from 21.35% in September to 12.34% in December. Repeating that 9.01-percentage-point slowdown gives roughly +3.33% in March and −5.69% in April–June. This forecast rests on the quarterly sales figures.

Dover booked $8.3 billion of orders against $8.5 billion of revenue in 2022. Bookings fell 11.1% while revenue rose 7.6%, aided by pricing (A, B, D). With December revenue still growing 7.54%, I expect existing orders to support March before weaker order intake reaches reported revenue in April–June.

Sales growth slowed from 30.14% in September to 4.49% in December. Strong preseason attachment orders accounted for much of the prior year's growth, alongside price increases in both segments (C, D). I expect March to remain above −5%, with the comparison against those orders pushing April–June sales down at least 5%.

Reported revenue growth fell from 16.55% in September to 6.57% in December. Repeating even two-thirds of that slowdown each quarter would put March near zero and April–June below −5%. Lower perpetual-license maintenance renewals are one source of pressure, though subscriptions partly offset them and software and related services represented 18% of revenue (A, B).

Revenue growth moved from +5.75% in September to −3.61% in December. Software and products accounted for 46% of nine-month revenue, and deals over $100,000 supplied 73% of that category (A, C). I expect March to stay near December's rate. With just 1.39 percentage points to the threshold, a modest shift in large-deal timing could produce the April–June crossing.

ACI's full-year revenue gain of $51.3 million (A), combined with declines of $10.3 million in September and $15.0 million in December, implies a $76.6 million year-over-year gain in the first half of 2022. That creates a tougher first-half comparison. I expect March near the two recent declines of about 3.2%, with a further 1.8 percentage points of weakness enough for an April–June crossing.

Product sales supplied $569.9 million of December's $648.2 million total. Their 38.6% growth came from selling prices as wholesale cost per gallon rose 54.4% (A). High heating costs also prompt conservation and customer losses (B). I expect pricing to keep March above −5%, with April–June exposed to a reversal if the year-over-year fuel price comparison turns negative.

Insight's net sales went from +3.55% in September to −2.47% in December. Hardware and software products made up 86% of reported sales (D). I expect March to remain just above −5%. At that sales mix, a further three percentage points of deterioration in product growth from December would be enough to cross in April–June if services growth holds steady.

Diodes reported 10.8% annual sales growth (A), but quarterly growth slowed from 10.57% in September to 3.34% in December. Repeating that 7.23-percentage-point slowdown puts March near −3.9%, still above the threshold, and April–June below −5%.

Union Pacific's revenue growth slowed from 17.97% to 7.80%. Annual freight revenue rose 14% on only 2% volume growth, with fuel surcharges and pricing contributing. Domestic and parcel demand softened in the fourth quarter (A, C). Another slowdown of December's size would leave March near −2.4%, with further weakening sufficient for an April–June crossing.

Covenant's revenue growth fell from 13.58% in September to 0.62% in December, and annual miles fell 3.5% (D). New warehousing customers added revenue (C), which could keep March above −5%. I expect the decline in miles to weigh more heavily on consolidated revenue by April–June.

CSX revenue growth slowed from 18.32% to 8.84%. Higher fuel recovery and export coal rates supported 2022 revenue even as chemical and export coal shipments declined (A–C). A repeat of the recent slowdown puts March near −0.6%. A smaller further slowdown could then take April–June below −5%.

J.B. Hunt's consolidated revenue growth fell from 22.05% to 4.37%. Higher revenue per load had supported annual growth in intermodal and truckload, while Integrated Capacity Solutions already had lower load volume (A, B). A slowdown of five percentage points per quarter, less than a third of the latest change, would put March near −0.6% and April–June near −5.6%.

Saia's January 24, 2022 general rate increase of 7.5% still benefits part of the March 2023 comparison, but April–June is the first full quarter compared against that higher rate. Shipments per workday had already fallen 0.8%, and revenue growth slowed from 18.39% to 6.26% (B, D). That pricing anniversary favors an April–June crossing.

Schneider's reported revenue growth fell from 15.98% to −0.83%. Network volumes were falling as demand moderated, while fuel surcharges contributed $417.7 million of the $995.7 million annual revenue increase (A, B, D). I expect March to remain above −5%, with weaker volume and a smaller surcharge contribution pushing April–June through the threshold.
